argument: Within human resting-state brain functional networks derived from fMRI, brain network flexibility (frequency of module-alignment change) is associated with brain network modularity (strength of community structure) under negative correlation; the association persists across different functional and anatomical parcellations and exceeds the correlation expected from randomized signals.
boundary: Evidence is limited to the reported resting-state fMRI sample, parcellation schemes, and analysis methods; transfer beyond them is unestablished.
claim: In human resting-state brain functional networks, flexibility and modularity are highly negatively correlated, and this negative association is not merely an artifact of the measurement method or parcellation choice.
conditions: resting-state fMRI data from 52 young adults
whole-brain network reconstructed with multiple functional and anatomical parcellations
comparison against randomized-signal and modularity-matched artificial networks
falsifier: Recompute flexibility and modularity in an independent resting-state fMRI sample and test whether their correlation remains significantly negative after controlling for network size, parcellation, and motion artifacts.
interpretation: The evidence supports a empirical association concerning human resting-state brain functional networks derived from fMRI.
